phrases.translation: Have you not seen ˹O Prophet˺ how your Lord dealt with the Army of the Elephant
phrases.text: Tabari reads this as beheld with the eye of the heart. They came from Yemen to destroy the Kaaba, and they were Abyssinians, with their commander Abraha, the man with the cleft lip.
phrases.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ كَيۡفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصۡحَٰبِ ٱلۡفِيلِ

phrases.translation: Did He not frustrate their scheme
phrases.text: Their plan to destroy the Kaaba was turned into an astrayness, so that they were diverted from what they meant and sought after.

phrases.translation: For He sent against them flocks of birds
phrases.text: Birds in scattered groups, one group following the other, from every side. The commentators differed over the word: some said the groups, some the swarms, some the numerous, and some the scattered.
They differed over what the birds looked like. Some said they were white, some black, some green with beaks like birds and paws like dogs, and some said they came out of the sea.

phrases.translation: that pelted them with stones of baked clay
phrases.text: The word is a foreign word for stone and clay. The stones were smaller than a chickpea and larger than a lentil, and each bird carried three, two in its feet and one in its beak. Some said the stones came from the lowest heaven, and Tabari says that report is not sound.

Tabari then tells why the punishment came. Abraha had built a church at San'a and resolved to turn the Arab pilgrimage away from the House. Abdul Muttalib went to him and asked for his two hundred camels back, and said: I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it.

phrases.translation: leaving them like chewed up straw
phrases.text: God made them like a crop the cattle have eaten and passed, so that it withered and fell apart. Tabari compares the tearing of their limbs and the scattering of their bodies to the scattering of what the cattle left behind.
The commentators differed over the word: some said the husk of the wheat, some the straw, some the leaf of the crop, and some the chaff that the wind blows away.
